column4: Upon pouring forth from Arafat, pilgrims are told to remember God at the sacred place; the transition from a completed movement into remembrance begins the ritual sequence continued in 2:199-200.
Pilgrims are told to depart where the people depart and then seek God's forgiveness, another completed movement followed by a deliberately Godward act before 2:200's completed rites.
Immediately after 2:200's person who asks only for this world, this speaker addresses “our Lord” for good in both this world and the Hereafter, correcting desire without denying earthly good.

When trade or amusement appears, people leave the Prophet standing; the ayah declares what is with God better and God the best provider, exposing the very worldward diversion that 62:9-10's work-worship cycle must govern.
The most balanced garden owner recalls that he had urged the others to glorify God; this is the first explicit summons away from acquisitive plotting and toward the Lord before 68:29-32.
When God's servant stands calling upon Him, the crowd nearly masses around him; standing and Godward invocation coincide in a scene especially close to “rise, exert yourself, and desire your Lord.”
The Prophet is commanded to keep an additional night vigil, with the hope that his Lord will raise him to a praised station; taxing worship, hoped-for divine gift, and rising are linked.
At the culmination of Joseph's long work and reunion, he names dominion and knowledge as his Lord's gifts, then asks the Creator to take him in submission and join him to the righteous.
At full maturity, the person asks his Lord for power to thank Him for His favor and to do righteous work pleasing to Him; received bounty becomes fresh, expressly directed labor.
Solomon responds to a bestowed ability by asking his Lord to enable gratitude, righteous work pleasing to Him, and entry into His mercy; gift, work, and desire all return to the Giver.

Dhu al-Qarnayn says what his Lord has established him in is better than the offered payment and asks the people to help with strength; the barrier project begins by preferring divine provision and directing collective labor.
The Lord of the heavens and earth is to be worshipped with steadfast perseverance in His worship, giving the section's repeated tiring service both its object and its sustaining command.
The Prophet must command his household to pray and persevere in it; God asks no provision from them but provides for them, sharply ordering exertion, desire, and gift around the Lord.
The Prophet says he is commanded to worship God with religion made sincere for Him, a direct statement of the exclusive direction expressed by the source section's fronted “to your Lord.”
The Prophet declares that God is the one he worships, making his devotion sincere for Him; the fronted object gives the same exclusive force as the section's وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ.
People were commanded only to worship God sincerely and uprightly, establish prayer, and give alms; exclusive orientation issues in repeated concrete acts.
Believers are commanded to call upon God with religion sincere for Him even when unbelievers dislike it, making exclusive Godward appeal a deliberate stance under opposition.
Because the Living One alone is God, people are commanded to call upon Him sincerely and praise the Lord of the worlds; exclusive address and lordship are joined explicitly.
Setting one's face at every place of worship and calling God with sincere religion turn bodily direction and invocation into a repeated exclusive practice.
Abraham turns his face toward the Creator of heavens and earth as an upright monotheist and rejects association, a vivid enacted counterpart to directing desire only toward the Lord.
The Prophet is commanded to set his face toward the religion uprightly and not be among the associators, expressing exclusive orientation as a sustained posture.
The command to set one's face toward the religion uprightly makes directedness itself the governing image of faithful action.
Whoever submits his face to God while doing good has his reward with his Lord; orientation, action, and divine recompense appear in one formulation.
The best religious course is to submit one's face to God while doing good and following Abraham, joining Godward orientation with active excellence.
One who submits his face to God while doing good has grasped the firmest handhold, and the outcome of all matters is to God; present action and final direction coincide.
Abraham says, “I am going to my Lord; He will guide me,” making movement toward the Lord both an intentional departure and an expectation of divine provision.
The tranquil soul is commanded to return to its Lord, satisfied and pleasing; the final Godward turn fulfills directed desire in mutual contentment.
The believer must follow the path of one who turns to God, and all will return to Him; chosen present direction is placed inside the unavoidable final return.
Those who avoid serving false powers and turn to God receive good news, giving the positive redirection that contrasts with the erected cult objects condemned in 5:90.
God chooses whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back, so deliberate reorientation toward Him is answered by divine guidance.
God guides to Himself whoever turns back, a concise promise that Godward direction draws a corresponding gift of guidance.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring good deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope; what is acquired is contrasted with work whose value remains before its Giver.

When called to go forth in God's path, some grow heavy toward the earth and prefer worldly life to the Hereafter; downward attachment and refusal of effort directly reverse the command to rise and labor toward the Lord.

Family, acquired wealth, feared commercial loss, and pleasing homes must not become dearer than God, His Messenger, and striving in His way; the ayah tests worldly acquisition against directed exertion.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from God's remembrance, a specific boundary keeping ordinary concerns inside the cycle of Godward attention.
A person gives up his very self seeking God's pleasure, making arduous action the embodied form of exclusively directed desire.
Those who spend their wealth seeking God's pleasure and inner firmness are compared to a garden yielding multiplied produce; direction, work, and abundant return are concretely connected.
Private counsel gains great reward when its charity, recognized good, or reconciliation is done seeking God's pleasure; the intended recipient determines the worth of practical work.
The Prophet's companions are seen bowing and prostrating while seeking bounty and pleasure from God, joining strenuous worship to the desire for divine gift.
The poor emigrants lose homes and wealth while seeking bounty and pleasure from God and supporting His cause, a concrete case of exhausting labor directed beyond worldly acquisition.
God offers a “trade” that saves from punishment, deliberately recasting the world of acquisition as an exchange whose direction and gain are divine.
The saving trade consists of faith and striving with wealth and lives in God's way, making costly work the concrete expression of the desire introduced in 61:10.
Reciting God's book, establishing prayer, and spending from His provision are people’s hope for a trade that will never perish; work and commerce are redirected toward lasting divine return.
“Your striving is diverse” states the problem at the heart of the section: exertion takes its value from the direction disclosed in the alternatives of 92:5-10.
The person who gives and remains mindful begins the positive course of striving whose outcome is ease in 92:7.
Affirming the best promise supplies the believed destination that distinguishes the giver's striving before 92:7 promises facilitation toward ease.
God will ease the giver and believer toward ease, linking the direction of effort in 92:5-6 with the ease that God provides.
Believers are commanded to bow, prostrate, worship their Lord, and do good so that they may prosper; bodily worship and useful work lead directly into 22:78's striving for God.
Believers must be mindful of God, seek a means toward Him, and strive in His way; direction toward God and strenuous activity are expressly combined.

Sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God, but piety does; the animals were subjected so believers may magnify Him, clarifying that an act's Godward direction lies in its intention rather than its material output.
The Lord answers the callers that He never lets any worker's work be lost, then names migration, expulsion, suffering, and fighting before promising reward from Himself.

A person in distress calls God lying, sitting, or standing, then passes on after relief as though never calling; temporary bodily orientation under need reverses the section's continuing cycle of devotion.
At sea, danger strips away every invoked object except God, but safe arrival on land is followed by turning away; the scene exposes an unstable, crisis-bound Godward direction.
When harm touches a person he calls his Lord turning to Him, but after divine favor he forgets and assigns rivals; gift becomes the occasion for reversed desire rather than renewed service.
People call their Lord while turning to Him under harm, yet after tasting mercy some associate partners; the change of circumstance reveals a direction that does not endure.
Whoever desires worldly reward receives from it and whoever desires Hereafter reward receives from it; the desired recompense distinguishes two orientations within mortal action.
Anyone desiring worldly reward is reminded that both worldly and Hereafter reward are with God, redirecting desire from one limited gift to the Giver who possesses both.
A catalog of desired people, treasure, animals, and fields is identified as worldly enjoyment, a concrete expansion of the section's “wide desire” to acquire the world.
Against 3:14's desired possessions, the Prophet asks whether he should announce something better: lasting gardens, purity, and pleasure with their Lord.
Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting; gift is distinguished from its enduring source.
The question about the greatest losers in works prepares a direct case of effort whose direction makes it futile, specified in 18:104.
Their striving goes astray in worldly life while they think they are doing well, a precise counterpart to exhausted work that never reaches its proper Lordward end.

Worldly life is play, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth and children whose growth withers, while the Hereafter holds punishment or divine forgiveness and pleasure; acquisitive effort is measured by what remains.

Monasticism was innovated while seeking God's pleasure, yet was not observed as it should have been; the ayah sets a boundary showing that a claimed Godward aim does not excuse a form of labor not faithfully kept.
The one who withholds and regards himself self-sufficient begins the opposite course of striving, reversing both giving and dependence upon the Lord.
Denying the best promise supplies the wrong destination behind the withholding and self-sufficiency of 92:8.
God will ease that person toward hardship, making the trajectory of misdirected effort the inverse of the ease promised in 92:7.
Those who make the balanced request of 2:201 have a share of what they earned, joining Godward asking to accountable human acquisition; its force depends on the preceding prayer.
The Prophet is to glorify God during the night and as the stars retreat, continuing 52:48's command to praise when rising into a repeated daily rhythm.
The Prophet must remember his Lord's name morning and evening, establishing the daily recurrence within which 76:26 places prolonged night worship.
Night prostration and long glorification continue the morning-evening remembrance of 76:25, giving sustained duration to the command to labor toward the Lord.
The Prophet is told to persevere because God's promise is true, seek forgiveness, and glorify his Lord evening and morning; endurance opens into a recurring cycle of Lordward acts.
